results.name: Kimsuky attacks targeting Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security, and international policy
results.description: The Kimsuky threat group has launched spear phishing campaigns targeting Ukrainian experts in diplomacy, security, and international policy through fraudulent international conference invitations and collaboration requests. This operation, dubbed GitPower, leverages legitimate development platforms like GitHub for malware distribution and data exfiltration. Attack vectors include malicious LNK files and fake Zoom installers, demonstrating links to previous CHM-based attack methodologies. The campaign appears to be state-sponsored cyber espionage focused on monitoring cooperation developments between South Korea and Ukraine. Organizations are advised to enhance EDR detection capabilities and implement threat hunting for suspicious LNK file execution, PowerShell abuse, and unauthorized GitHub communications.

results.name: The XG Files: Falcon C2 Flying Under The (Browser) Radar
results.description: A sophisticated command and control framework named Falcon (also known as XG or Xiàng Gē) has been identified operating entirely within browser contexts through malicious JavaScript. The framework compromises webmail portals and government web applications, enabling attackers to sideload malicious Chrome and Firefox extensions that steal passwords, emails, session cookies, and communications. Falcon also delivers an implant called Antino, which uses Microsoft OneDrive as a C2 channel. Between March and May 2026, government entities in one Middle Eastern country and four Southeast Asian countries were compromised, specifically targeting ministries of foreign affairs, defense, interior, and law enforcement agencies. The framework shares significant overlap with PeckBirdy and demonstrates advanced capabilities including browser proxy functionality, download interception, network traffic hijacking, and credential harvesting. results.name: SCKit Worm Installs Rogue ScreenConnect Clients and Session Cookie Relays Across Hundreds of Endpoints
results.description: On November 11, 2026, operators exploited cloud-hosted ScreenConnect panels to deploy attacker-controlled clients and the SCKit toolkit across 288 hosts in 48 organizations. ConnectWise disabled five third-party extensions as a precaution but had not identified the initial access vector. The attack involved two stages: spreading from infected endpoints to technician workstations via session cookie theft, then laterally to other accessible endpoints. SCKit consists of 16 PowerShell and batch scripts delivered as encrypted payloads, using system UUIDs as decryption keys. The toolkit installs rogue ScreenConnect clients, creates persistence mechanisms through scheduled tasks, and attempts console takeover. While endpoint infections succeeded, the technician workstation compromise functionality failed in all observed cases. The worm includes sophisticated features like browser cookie extraction, session replay, and automated payload distribution through ScreenConnect's Shared Toolbox.

results.name: The global socket: how threat actors are weaponizing GSocket for stealthy C2
results.description: Multiple threat actors have been deploying GSocket, an open source remote access tool, on compromised Linux servers to maintain persistent access even after initial vulnerabilities are patched. The activity increased 356.2% from March through August 2026, primarily targeting web applications and hosting environments, with education and research sectors representing 30.7% of affected organizations. GSocket relays traffic through a shared public network, eliminating traditional C2 infrastructure that defenders could block. Threat actors exploit internet-facing applications, deploy GSocket with renamed processes in memory-backed directories, establish persistence through cron and systemd, and in some cases escalate privileges using CVE-2026-43284. The tool's outbound-only connections and shared relay infrastructure make it particularly difficult to detect and remediate through conventional methods.

results.name: Beware of Phishing Email Disguised as Quotation Inquiry (SnakeKeylogger)
results.description: A phishing campaign disguised as quotation inquiry requests has been observed, where attackers impersonate purchasing team material management personnel requesting quote confirmations. The emails contain compressed attachments that, when extracted, reveal JavaScript files. These execute obfuscated PowerShell scripts that decrypt and run multi-stage payloads using AES-256-CBC encryption and XOR operations. The attack chain utilizes process hollowing techniques to inject the final payload into aspnet_compiler.exe. The ultimate malware is SnakeKeylogger, an infostealer that collects web browser credentials, system information, and keylogging data, exfiltrating it via SMTP or Telegram to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

results.name: The Rise of LLMjacking: How Attackers Monetize Compromised Cloud and Model Resources
results.description: Google Threat Intelligence Group identified multiple incidents where attackers hijacked enterprise Large Language Model (LLM) access in a tactic called LLMJacking. These intrusions affected organizations across financial services, retail, technology, and transportation sectors in North America, South America, and Asia Pacific. Unlike cryptojacking's gradual resource consumption, LLMJacking can generate fraudulent cloud charges exceeding $100,000 per day within hours, with cumulative bills reaching $1 million before access revocation. Attackers obtain initial access through exposed cloud credentials, API keys, and service account tokens, then escalate privileges and deploy proxy infrastructure to resell stolen compute capacity through underground marketplaces operated by LLM Mixers, who aggregate and redistribute unauthorized model access to subscribers.

results.name: Off the Rails: Inside an Exposed Silent Lynx Server
results.description: An exposed open directory belonging to Silent Lynx, a Central Asia-focused espionage cluster, revealed the group's operations through October 2026. The directory contained tooling, data from active intrusions into government and critical infrastructure, and an AI agent used by the operator. The operator maintained persistent access to transport networks, collected government correspondence at scale including defence-related documents, and compromised a government geospatial platform. Implants matched known Laplas and Chvost families, alongside unreported variants. Lures impersonating Turkmenistan Railways were prepared for an upcoming campaign. A self-hosted AI agent running DeepSeek handled reconnaissance, collection and log cleanup. The operator worked in Russian with test traffic originating from residential Kazakhtelecom connections, supporting a Kazakhstan nexus assessment. Multiple OPSEC failures exposed the operation including storing everything on one server and leaving developer paths in binaries.

results.name: Citrus Ransomware: tactics, techniques, procedures, and links to Toy Ghouls
results.description: Citrus Ransomware represents a hybrid threat combining traditional infrastructure compromise techniques with modern evasion methods and AI-powered automation. The group gains initial access through compromised contractor accounts, using stolen credentials for VPN or RDP connections. Attackers employ VLESS tunnels disguised as HTTPS traffic and leverage large language models to generate commands and scripts. They exploit vulnerabilities like CVE-2026-54121 for privilege escalation, utilize tools including mimikatz and Snaffler for credential theft, and deploy the Sn00py ransomware via Group Policy Objects. The operation involves disabling security solutions, clearing event logs, and harvesting Telegram session data before encryption. The malware uses RSA-2048 and ChaCha20 algorithms, appending .citrus extensions to encrypted files. Links to Toy Ghouls suggest possible connections between Russian-speaking groups targeting Russian organizations exclusively.

results.name: Beyond the clipboard: The evolving tradecraft of ClickFix
results.description: Threat actors continue to evolve ClickFix tactics, moving beyond simple clipboard-based social engineering to more sophisticated attack chains. Recent campaigns leverage malvertising through typosquatting, SEO poisoning, and compromised websites to deliver fake verification prompts. These attacks now employ elaborate PowerShell scripts with animated progress bars to mimic legitimate security checks. Observed payloads include Node.js-based RATs like DuskDesk, lateral movement techniques targeting domain controllers via WinRM and SSH tunnels, and steganographic delivery chains hiding executables within PNG files. Some campaigns utilize browser-cache-seeded attacks that detect the victim's browser and retrieve staged payloads from cached files. Defense requires user training to recognize social engineering, application control policies, and behavioral monitoring for suspicious command execution patterns and persistence mechanisms.

results.name: From WhatsApp to SYSTEM: Inside the VulcanRAT207.A Intrusion Chain
results.description: A sophisticated multi-stage intrusion chain begins with a WhatsApp-delivered financial document lure carrying Statement.exe. The malware employs NRV2E compression to conceal its true payload, which performs extensive host screening before attempting privilege elevation via COM-based techniques. Using PoolParty Variant 7 injection, the loader transfers execution into the Windows Task Scheduler process under LocalSystem authority. A downloader shellcode retrieves a compound bundle from a remote server, which deploys through a reflective loader. The deployment stage utilizes a signed GoFly driver to terminate Baidu security processes, establishes persistence via DLL side-loading with a legitimate Intel-signed VulkanInfo executable, and launches a WebSocket-based remote access trojan.
